title: Biases
text: A bias is a systematic and predictable deviation from rational judgment that comes from cognitive, emotional or social factors. It is not a theory of why people behave the way they do. It is just a systematic average error.

title: Biases
text:
Established Biases

Default Bias

People tend to stick with the pre-set option, even when switching is cheap (e.g. automatic enrollment into a retirement plan strongly raises participation).



Framing

Decisions depend on how options are presented (e.g. as a gain or as a loss), even if the outcomes are identical.



Overconfidence

Miscalibration / over-precision: Belief that you know more than you actually do
Better-than-average effect: Belief that you are better than the median person



Overreaction

Investors put too much weight on new information, so prices move too far and later reverse.



Recency Bias

Recent events get more weight than older ones when forming expectations (e.g. expecting high returns to continue after a bull market).



Home Bias

Investors prefer local and familiar stocks \(\to\) people invest too much in the home country
Makes people feel safe but in reality exposes them to idiosyncratic risk
Example: Enron employees had 62% of their retirement plan assets in company stock \(\to\) Enron went bankrupt, employees lost their job and retirement income.



Familiarity Bias

People tend to prefer things they are already familiar with



Herd Behavior

Even if fake news is false, investors may follow the crowd, assuming that others have more accurate information.



Social Proof

Social proof is the tendency to conform to the behavior of others



Experience

Personally lived experiences shape beliefs and risk taking more than other available information (e.g. people who lived through low stock returns invest less in stocks).



Culture

Cultural background (e.g. trust, individualism) systematically shapes financial decisions (e.g. people with low trust are less likely to hold stocks).



Hindsight Bias

Tendency to believe that past events were predicted better than they actually were (“I knew it all along”)



Confirmation Bias

Interpret, recall, search for information in a way that confirms prior beliefs or values



Self-attribution Bias

Attributing success to own abilities/effort, while ascribing failure to external factors



Present Bias

Preferring a smaller immediate reward over a larger later reward, in a way that does not only represent the time difference.

text:

Scott Cunningham
mixtape.scunning.com


Introduces the main causal inference designs such as matching, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences with worked examples in R and Stata.

Nick Huntington-Klein
theeffectbook.net


Explains research design and causal identification with an intuitive focus and fewer formulas, using causal diagrams to build up each method.

Joshua D. Angrist
learn.mru.org


A free video course on Marginal Revolution University that teaches the five core tools of causal inference in short, humorous lessons with a kung fu theme.

Joshua D. Angrist, Jörn-Steffen Pischke
Book


A more technical graduate text that treats regression, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity from the design-based perspective.


Mastering ’Metrics: The Path from Cause to Effect (2014)
Joshua D. Angrist, Jörn-Steffen Pischke
Book


An accessible introduction by the same authors to the five core tools of applied econometrics: randomized trials, regression, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences.


Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach (2008)
Jeffrey M. Wooldridge
Book


A standard introductory textbook that develops linear regression and inference step by step and extends them to time series and panel data with many applied examples.


Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data (2010, 2nd edition)
Jeffrey M. Wooldridge
Book


A rigorous graduate text on estimation and inference with cross section and panel data, covering instrumental variables, GMM, fixed and random effects and nonlinear models.


Freakonomics: A Rogue Economist Explores the Hidden Side of Everything (2005)
Steven D. Levitt, Stephen J. Dubner
Book


A popular science book that uses economic reasoning and data to separate correlation from causation in everyday questions such as cheating, crime and parenting.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text: A regression discontinuity design (RDD) uses one or more jumps in how a policy is assigned to estimate a causal effect (Wooldridge 2025). It cannot answer every causal question, but where it applies, its results are almost as convincing as those of a randomized trial (Angrist and Pischke 2015, 166–67).

title: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Sharp RDD
The treatment status is deterministic and discontinuous function of a covariate \(X_i\): \[
D_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X_i \geq c \\ 0 & \text{if } X_i < c \end{cases}
\] It is deterministic, because knowing \(X_i\) means knowing \(D_i\) and it is discontinuous, because \(D_i\) does not change until \(X_i\) reaches \(c\), no matter how close \(X_i\) gets to it. As a result, there is no value of \(X_i\) at which we observe both treated and untreated units (Angrist and Pischke 2009, 251–52).
The treatment effect is the ATE at the cutoff, \(E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid X_i = c]\).

title: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Fuzzy RDD
Crossing the cutoff only changes the probability or expected value of treatment conditional on the running variable. So some units below \(c\) are treated or some units above \(c\) are not. The discontinuity becomes an instrumental variable for treatment status (Angrist and Pischke 2009, 259). \[
P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) = \begin{cases} g_1(X_i) & \text{if } X_i \geq c \\ g_0(X_i) & \text{if } X_i < c \end{cases}, \quad \text{where } g_1(c) \neq g_0(c)
\] The functions \(g_0(X_i)\) and \(g_1(X_i)\) can take any form as long as they differ at \(c\), and a bigger difference is better because it gives a stronger first stage. We assume \(g_1(c) > g_0(c)\), so crossing the cutoff makes treatment more likely (Angrist and Pischke 2009, 260).
The treatment effect is the jump in the outcome divided by the jump in the treatment probability at \(c\). This ratio is the LATE for compliers at the cutoff.

title: The Overlapping Generations Model (OLG)
text:
The basic overlapping generations model with capital accumulation was introduced by Diamond (1965), however this summary is mostly based on De la Croix and Michel (2002).
In the benchmark Diamond economy each household lives for two periods. When young, it works, earns a wage, consumes part of this income and saves the rest. When old, it is retired and consumes the gross return on the savings it made when young. Through these individual saving decisions, the young generation builds the capital stock that firms use in the next period.

title: The Overlapping Generations Model (OLG)
text:
Household Problem

Preferences
The lifetime utility of an individual born at \(t\) depends on consumption when young and when old:
\[
U_t = u(c_t, d_{t+1})
\]


Budget Constraints
\[
\text{Young:}\quad c_t + s_t = w_t
\]
\[
\text{Old:}\quad d_{t+1} = R_{t+1}\, s_t \;\Rightarrow\; s_t = \frac{d_{t+1}}{R_{t+1}}
\]
\(R_{t+1}\) is the gross return on savings. Substituting \(s_t\) gives the lifetime budget constraint:
\[
c_t + \frac{d_{t+1}}{R_{t+1}} = w_t
\]


Optimization
The household takes \(w_t\) and \(R_{t+1}\) as given and solves
\[
\max_{c_t,\, d_{t+1} \ge 0} \; u(c_t, d_{t+1}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad w_t = c_t + \frac{d_{t+1}}{R_{t+1}}
\]
\[
\mathcal{L} = u(c_t, d_{t+1}) + \lambda_t \left( w_t - c_t - \frac{d_{t+1}}{R_{t+1}} \right)
\]
F.O.C.:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial c_t} = u_{c_t} - \lambda_t = 0 \qquad (1)
\]
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial d_{t+1}} = u_{d_{t+1}} - \frac{\lambda_t}{R_{t+1}} = 0 \qquad (2)
\]
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda_t} = w_t - c_t - \frac{d_{t+1}}{R_{t+1}} = 0 \qquad (3)
\]
From (1), \(\lambda_t = u_{c_t}\). Replacing in (2):
\[
u_{d_{t+1}} = \frac{u_{c_t}}{R_{t+1}}
\]
The marginal utility of one unit consumed when old equals the marginal utility of the \(1/R_{t+1}\) units given up when young.

title: The Overlapping Generations Model (OLG)
text:
Firms Problem

Technology
Firms produce output with capital \(K_t\) and labor \(L_t\) using a production function \(F(K_t, L_t)\) with constant returns to scale. For \(\lambda > 0\):
\[
F(\lambda K_t, \lambda L_t) = \lambda F(K_t, L_t)
\]
Setting \(\lambda = \frac{1}{L_t}\) gives the intensive form with capital per worker \(k_t = \frac{K_t}{L_t}\):
\[
f(k_t) = F(k_t, 1) = \frac{F(K_t, L_t)}{L_t} \iff F(K_t, L_t) = L_t f(k_t)
\]
The marginal products then only depend on \(k_t\):
\[
\frac{\partial F(K_t, L_t)}{\partial K_t} = f'(k_t), \qquad \frac{\partial F(K_t, L_t)}{\partial L_t} = f(k_t) - k_t f'(k_t)
\]


Optimization
Firms rent capital at the rental rate \(q_t\) and hire labor at the wage \(w_t\). They take both prices as given and maximize profits:
\[
\max_{K_t, L_t} \; \pi_t = F(K_t, L_t) - w_t L_t - q_t K_t
\]
F.O.C.:
\[
\frac{\partial \pi_t}{\partial K_t} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; f'(k_t) = q_t
\]
\[
\frac{\partial \pi_t}{\partial L_t} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; f(k_t) - k_t f'(k_t) = w_t
\]
Each factor is paid its marginal product. Capital depreciates at rate \(\delta\), so the gross return on savings is the rental rate plus the undepreciated capital:
\[
R_t = 1 + r_t = q_t + 1 - \delta \;\Rightarrow\; q_t = r_t + \delta
\]

title: Heuristics
text: Heuristics are mental shortcuts or rules of thumb used to simplify decision-making.

title: Heuristics
text:
Established Heuristics

Representativeness

People judge how likely something is based on how representative it is
Example: In Ireland only 10% of the population have red hair. In other parts around the world only 1% \(\to\) People connect red hair to Ireland
Law of Small Numbers: People tend to think that a small sample must be representative for the whole population
Gambler’s Fallacy: Consider a series of 10 tosses of a fair coin that have all landed “heads”. Many believe the next coin toss is more likely to result in “tails”. Tversky and Kahneman (1974): Chance is commonly viewed as a self-correcting process in which a deviation in one direction induces a deviation in the opposite direction to restore equilibrium.



Availability

Judging probability based on how easily examples come to mind (e.g. fear of flying after hearing about plane crashes).



Attention

People have limited attention and focus on salient information, so they buy assets that grab their attention (e.g. stocks in the news or with extreme returns).



Anchoring

Relying heavily on an initial piece of information (e.g. adjusting estimates based on irrelevant anchors like random numbers).
In many situations, people make estimates by starting from an initial value that is adjusted to yield the final answer.
Adjustment from the anchor is usually insufficient.
Example: “Suggested retail price” influences perceived value



Adjustment

People start from a known value and adjust it step by step, but stop too early, so the final estimate stays biased towards the starting point.



Menu Dependence / The Decoy Effect

Choice between A and B. Some people choose A, some choose B
Add decoy option C that is strictly dominated by one of the other two options.
Fractions of people who choose A and B should stay the same. BUT they actually change
Example: The Economist subscription model. Added decoy option \(\to\) More people choose the dominating option.



Trend Extrapolation

Forming forecasts, beliefs and expectations by extrapolating past trends

title: Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
In some settings, the outcomes of a treated and a control group would move in parallel without treatment. In that case, a post-treatment path of the treated group that departs from the trend of the control group may point to a treatment effect (Angrist and Pischke 2015, 180).




References

Angrist, Joshua D., and Jörn-Steffen Pischke. 2015. Mastering ’Metrics: The Path from Cause to Effect. Princeton University Press.
